HOW DO YOU ACHIEVE HIGH QUALITY SOLDER JOINTS? 
The process of producing high quality solder joints is 
similar to the process of learning how to ride a bicycle. 
If you do not understand the fundamentals, it is virtually 
impossible. However, once you understand and imple- 
ment the basics, the results will follow. The goal of all 
SMT process engineers is to repeatedly produce high 
quality solder joints that have fine grain structure and 
excellent wetting characteristics, as shown in the figure 
below:

CONTROL VARIABLES 
In order to produce high quality solderjoints, all process 
variables must be in control. The five general process 
variables (l) that need to be in control include the mate- 
rials, machines, manpower, methods, and the environ- 
ment. If the process variables are not in control, there is 
a very good chance that soldering defects will exist. 
Let’s take a closer look at each. 
MATERIALS 
The materials must meet functional specifications so 
that the product will perform to specification. Of equal 
importance is the solderability of the assembly. The 
solder paste/flux system must be compatible with the 
base materials of the parts to be soldered. The solder 
paste and parts should be as fresh as possible to enhance 
solderability. 
MACHINES 
The machines used in the process must be able to perform 
to their specifications. The machines should operate 
within the range for which they are designed. Pushing a 
machine beyond its operating limits will ultimately cause 
a problem. The machines must be reliable and service- 
able. 
MANPOWER 
The manpower must be properly trained. All machines in 
the line require knowledgeable operators and mainte- 
nance personnel. A machine is only as good as the person 
operating it. 
METHODS 
The methods and procedures must be defined and strictly 
adhered to. Inventory procedures should be implemented 
to ensure that components and boards do not stay on the 
shelf too long. Problems should be fully documented 
including all data that pertains to it. 
ENVIRONMENT 
Finally, the processing environment must be controlled. 
This includes both the environment inside and outside of 
the machines. For example, if the humidity in the solder- 
ing area is too high, this can cause the solder paste to 
absorb moisture, whichmay cause problems duringreflow . 
If the temperature in the room is not controlled, the 
thermal profile in the reflow oven may be affected, which 
again may cause a defect. 
The purpose of this text is to address one aspect of high 
quality SMT soldering, the reflow process. 
Producing high quality solder joints 
requires that five general process 
variables need to be in control; the 
materials, machines, manpower, 
methods, and the environment.

WHAT IS THE IMPORTANCE OF THE PROFILE? 
I I I I I I 1; I :I I I I I 
In order to fully understand Surface Mount Technology 
(SMT) reflow, one needs to have an understanding of 
what is being accomplished. One can take too simplistic 
a viewpoint in that all you need to do is to heat solder 
to a temperature greater than its melting point. One can 
also take too complicated a viewpoint in believing that a 
certain wavelength of infrared (IR) is required, or that a 
certain percentage of convection is required. Perhaps the 
most astute comment made on surface mount reflow was 
by an individual whom had just completed an evaluation 
of vapor phase, panel IR, and lamp IR equipment nearly 
five years ago. After coming up with virtually identical 
soldering defect results on all three types of soldering 
equipment, the following comment was made: “If you 
could hit the correct reflow profile using buckets of hot 
water, you would accomplish high quality, low defect 
solder joints.” Although the above comment was made 
in jest (hot water is not quite hot enough to reflow solder), 
there is considerable truth to what was said. 
I 
REFLOW PROFILE REQUIREMENT 
High quality, low defect soldering requires identifying 
the optimum temperature profile for reflowing the solder 
paste, and repeating over and over. Every solder joint on 
every board, needs to be heated similarily if the desired 
soldering results are to be accomplished. It does not 
matter how you apply the heat to the solder joint. What 
does matter is that the heat is applied to the solder joint 
in a controlled manner. The heating and cooling rise 
rates must be compatible with the solder paste and 
components. The amount of time that the assembly is 
exposed to certain temperatures must be defined and 
maintained. In other words, the solder reflow profile 
must first be defined and then maintained.

TYPICAL PROFILE 
A typical profile consists of a preheat, dryout, and reflow 
section (zone) where different heating rates are used. In 
the preheat section, the goal is to fully preheat the SMT 
assembly to temperatures generally between 100°C to 
150°C. The most critical parameter in the preheat section 
is to minimize the rate of rise to less than 2”C/second. 
The main concern is minimizing thermal shock on the 
components of the assembly. Multilayer ceramic chip 
capacitors can be vulnerable to cracking if heated too 
fast. Solder paste can spatter also, if heated too fast. 
The second heating section, referred to as the dryout, 
soak, or preflow zone, is used primarily to ensure that 
the solder paste is fully dried before hitting reflow 
temperatures. This zone also acts as a flux activation 
zone for some solder pastes. Solder reflow is accom- 
plished in the reflow zone, where the solder paste is 
elevated to a temperature greater than the melting point 
of the solder. For 63/37 Eutectic solder, the melting 
temperature is 183°C. This temperature must be ex- 
ceeded by approximately 20°C to ensure quality reflow. 
The amount of time the solder joint is above the melting 
point is referred to as the “wetting time”. The wetting 
time is normally 30 to 60 seconds for most pastes. If the 
wetting time is excessive, intermetallics may occur in 
the joint, which result in brittle solder joints. In sum- 
mary, define the profile, and hit it.

HOW MANY HEATING ZONES ARE REQUIRED? 
This question frequently arrives and can be a source of 
confusion. One theory is that if ten zones are good, then 
twenty zones are better. While in theory this may be true, 
in practicality it may not be true. While it improves the 
flexibility of oven, it also adds to the complexity and 
makes oven set-up more difficult. 
Let’s review this question from the standpoint of how 
many zones are really needed. Reflowing solder paste 
typically requires two or three different heating rates to 
accomplish the process. In the figure below, there are 
three “typical” profile bands for RMA, water soluble, 
and no-clean solder pastes. These profiles are rather 
generic, and one should consult with their solder paste 
vendor to determine the desired profile. All of the pastes 
in the figure could be successfully reflowed using 
three zones.

Edge heating zones become significant when edge con-

WHAT IS THE PROFILE PROCESS BAND? 
In reality the profile is not a line, but rather a band or 
process window.(*) The size of the band is defined by the 
range of temperature deviation that can occur during 
reflow and yield high quality results. This is indicated 
by the crosshatched area shown in the figure. In the 
example, the profile band size is indicated as 25°C. 
The actual size of the band will vary depending upon 
solder paste, component type, and circuit board material. 
SOLDER SPATTER 
AND SOLDER BALLS 
CAUSED BY INSUF- 
FICIENT DRYING. 
BURNT BOARDS, 
DEWET SOLDER 
fi COLD SOLDER 
JOINTS, DULL 
SOLDER JOINTS 
(TOO COLD) 
REFLOW SOLDERING DEFECTS 
If the product temperature profile is not maintained 
within the band, a defect will occur. Chip capacitors 
may crack if the rise rate in the preheat zone is exces- 
sive. Solder spatter and solder balls may occur if drying 
is excessive or insufficient. If drying is excessive, the 
solder paste may skin over and not allow any of the 
volatiles to escape. As the temperature of the solder joint 
continues to heat, the vapor pressure increases until the 
solder joint virtually explodes as the gases escape rap- 
idly. The result is solder spatter and solder balls. If the 
preheat is insufficient, solder spatter and balls may occur 
in the reflow zone when higher heating rates occur. It is 
critical that the paste is dried at low controlled heating 
rates. In the reflow zone, insufficient heat will result in 
non-reflowed or partially reflowed solder joints. The 
joints will have a dull, rough surface finish in this case. 
Excessive heating in the reflow zone may result in burnt 
boards, damaged components, or possibly solder 
dewetting. In a dewet solder joint, the solder is reflowed 
but it is pulled away from the pad or the component lead. 
DEFINE THE BAND 
The profile band needs to be defined for the given SMT 
assembly. To define this band, one should be aware of 
not only the solder paste requirements, but also any 
specific requirements of components or the circuit board 
material. The process band width is defined as the total 
deviation in temperature that can occur and yield reliable 
results. 
OVEN PERFORMANCE 
From a process standpoint, the reflow oven must be able 
to produce consistent results within the reflow profile 
band. The user should be aware of all variables that 
influence the band. These variables may be defined as 
product related and oven related. By far the most critical 
product related non-uniformity is that created by large 
mass differences on the product. Since it is easier to heat 
an area that has no components as compared with an area 
with large components, temperature differentials will 
exist on the product. Machine related non-uniformities 
such as repeatability under product load and edge-to- 
center and front-to-back product heating uniformities 
must also be considered. To achieve high quality, low 
defect soldering results, the sum of all the non-uniformi- 
ties must fall within the defined reflow profile band. 
In reality the profile is not a line, but rather 
a range of temperatures all solder joints 
must be exposed. 
The total temperature deviation from 
component thermal mismatch, oven load- 
ing, and oven uniformity must be within 
the band.

WHAT ARE THE CAUSES OF NON-UNIFORM HEATING? 
In order to fully comprehend the capability to heat within 
the defined process band, one needs to better understand 
the causes of heating non-uniformities. The three main 
causes of non-uniform heating in the SMT reflow pro- 
cess include mass differential on the product, conveyor 
and heater edge effects, and product loading. 
MASS DIFFERENTIAL 
The amount of temperature rise of a product as it travels 
through a heating zone depends upon a number of 
variables. The temperature rise of an object subjected to 
heat is determined by the following equation: 
AT = Q x AX t / (M x Cp) 
WHERE: 
AT = Product Temperature Rise (“C) 
Q = Heat Absorbed (w/cmz) 
A = Exposed Area (cm2) 
t = Heating Dwell Time (seconds) 
M = Mass of Object (kg) 
Cp = Specific Heat (w-sec/kg-”C) 
The mass (M) times the specific heat (Cp) is often referred 
to as thermal mass. Greater thermal mass requires more 
heat to achieve a given temperature rise. In the figure 
shown below, the area populated with the PLCC’s has 
considerably more thermal mass per unit area than the 
area with the discrete components. This area will be more 
difficult to heat. The non-uniformity caused by thermal 
mass differential may be measured by thermocoupling a 
lead on the largest and smallest device, and running a 
profile.

A second main cause of non-uniform product heating is 
the oven heating pattern. This can be caused by edge 
effects on the heaters (less heat at the end) or by heat 
sinking of the conveyor system. The edge effect may be 
caused by insufficient airflow around the edges of the 
machine, or by non-uniformities that are inherent in the 
heaters. The heat sinking of the conveyor is really amass

uniformity may be measured by thermocoupling a bare 
board over a matrix of points, and running a profile. The 
matrix should include points on the board edges (front, 
back, left, and right), and the center of the board. 
OVEN REPEATABILITY 
Repeatability refers to the oven’s capability to repeat a 
given profile. Repeatability is affected by machine 
loading. The figure below shows a typical product

Reflow soldering in a nitrogen atmosphere is becoming

fluxes to remove oxides during the reflow process. The 
future trend is moving away from strong fluxes in the 
paste. The future trends include two major process 
changes that are driving the need for reflow in nitrogen 
atmospheres; fine pitch soldering and no-clean fluxes.

FINE PITCH REFLOW SOLDERING 
Fine pitch soldering presents many challenges. In order 
to obtain satisfactory paste print definition, the particle 
sizes of tin and lead are becoming smaller. As the 
particles become smaller, the ratio of surface area to 
volume of the particles increases. This can be shown by:

GREATER SURFACE AREA WITH SMALLER PARTICLES THAN

Thus, as particles sizes decrease, the ratio increases. 
With more available surface area in the solder paste, 
there is a greater tendency towards oxidation. Keep in 
mind that oxidation is a function of the metals involved, 
the temperatures of the metal, the exposed surface area, 
and the amount of oxygen present. The only variable 
that one can control is the amount of oxygen present. 
This can only be done through proper oven design. 
NO-CLEAN SOLDERING 
The second technology change that is driving the need 
towards nitrogen atmospheres is the greater usage of no- 
clean pastes. The rapid trend away from solvent cleaning 
is creating this and other needs. No-clean soldering 
requires a tight control of the process. All of the compo- 
nents and boards must be highly solderable. The reflow 
process must not add any significant oxidation to the 
process. The fluxes used are very weak, and do not have 
aggressive oxide cleaning action. In addition, there is no 
cleaning that would remove any solder balls from the 
product. These solder balls eventually can create short 
circuits on the product if they are not removed. Reflowing 
in a high purity nitrogen environment reduces the possi- 
bility of creating solder balls.

WHAT ARE THE STEPS IN THE SELECTION PROCESS? 
When selecting reflow equipment, it is important to take 
into consideration all aspects that may affect the process 
and production. Try to avoid becoming too focussed on 
one issue, such as populated uniformity, as it may not 
lead you to the optimum decision. The recommended 
steps in the selection process are described in the follow- 
ing paragraphs. 
DEFINE PROCESS BAND WIDTH 
The first step is to define the acceptable process profile 
band width for your SMT assemblies. Try to be as 
accurate as possible when defining the band. If the band 
is too restrictive, some aspect of production will be 
negatively affected. If the band is too loose, a defect will 
show up in the process. The band width should be 
defined as a range of temperatures ("C) that the entire 
profile must fall within. Refer to page 4 for a more 
detailed description. 
DEFINE HEATING NON-UNIFORMITIES 
The next step is to define causes of heating non-unifor- 
mities that may occur in the process. These non-unifor- 
mities are caused by mass differential, oven uniformity, 
and oven repeatability under production loading condi- 
tions. A set of tests must be conducted with the desired 
product on the oven in question. The sum of the non- 
uniformities ("C) must be less than the profile band width 
defined in the first step. Refer to page 5 for a more 
detailed description.

If a nitrogen atmosphere is required for solderability or 
no-clean processing (see page lo), one needs to consider 
the purity required and the gas consumption. Be careful 
how the purity is measured, such that it is not measured 
at the gas inlet. 
REVIEW CONVEYOR DESIGN 
The conveying mechanism is perhaps the most over- 
looked aspect of equipment selection. One needs to 
define whether a mesh conveyor or an edge type is 
required. Typically edge conveyors are used for in-line 
processing or if double-sided assembly is required. The 
most important issue with edge conveyors is the ability 
for the conveyor to remain straight to avoid dropping 
product. 
RELIABILITY/SERVICEABILITY 
Once a machine is placed into service, it is critical that it 
remains operational. Evaluate the product design from a 
structural as well as a functional standpoint. Is the oven 
designed to withstand the rigors of production? Review 
the product manuals, drawings, and spare parts lists. 
Find out where the nearest servicing center is located. Is 
training available? These are the questions that must be 
asked during the selection process. 
INTERFACING REQUIREMENTS 
Conveyor and control interfacing requirements may also 
be an important selection issue. Make sure that the edge 
conveyor fixed rail justification is the same as the pick- 
and-place equipment. Ask questions about networking 
machines to a host and product flow control schemes if 
needed.

repeatability off 2.5”C will occur if the bulk chamber 
is within this defined band. 
The ability to operate within this wide band has two 
significant advantages. The first is that the oven may 
be loaded down to levels up to 80% load. The second is 
that profile changeover times are reduced significantly. 
Loading may begin when all oven temperatures are 
within f 25°C of setpoint. This requires far less time to 
achieve the “ready” state than if the “ready” process 
window was f 3”C, which is often the case inreflow oven 
operation. Warm-up times of less than 15 minutes occur. 
Profile changeover times are 3 to 5 minutes for profile 
increases of under 40”C, and under 10 minutes for profile 
decreases of under 40°C. Even in the worst case of going 
from a reflow profile to an adhesive cure profile, the 
changeover time is under 15 minutes.

IR/CONVECTION OVEN WITH NITROGEN ATMOSPHERE 
PREHEAT TOP (IR1) 
Infrared ovens do not require high quantities of flow to 
accomplish reflow. The predominant heat transfer oc- 
curs with IR, which does not require any flow to transfer 
the heat. The flow in the oven is used to provide some of 
the benefits of convection, which includes improving 
populated board uniformity and volatile removal. The 
amount of flow in the oven is more related to the quantity 
required to accomplish a high purity nitrogen environ-

convection oven.

NITROGEN OVEN DESCRIPTION 
The 4470XN from Research, Inc. is an example of an IR 
dominant oven that provides a high purity nitrogen 
environment at low flow levels. The system uses a 
proprietary gas flow distribution method through the 
chamber walls to uniformly blanket the chamber with the 
process nitrogen. A slight positive pressure inside the 
chamber helps minimize external room effects and helps 
keep oxygen out of the chamber. Entry and exit purge 
sections are present to provide a nitrogen curtain at the 
chamber entrance and exit, which also assists in keeping 
oxygen out of the chamber. Flow meter controlled 
venturi exhausts are used to balance the flow in the 
system and to remove process volatiles. 
PREHEAT BOTTOM (IR2) 
The gas system is non-recirculatory, in that the gas is 
used once and then expended. This has the advantage 
that process contaminants are not recirculated which 
helps maintain high nitrogen purity levels. The heat 
chamber is accessible by unfastening six clamps and 
elevating the top heater vertically through the use of a 
crank mechanism. Purity levels of 20 PPM (over in- 
coming purity level) are attainable in all heating zones. 
Flow rates are in the 1200 to 1600 cubic feet per hour 
(34 to 45 cubic meters per hour) range. Machines in the 
field are experiencing total purity levels of 10-15 PPM 
(including incoming) at flow rates of 1300 cubic feet per 
hour (37 cubic meters per hour). These purity levels are 
measured with the machine fully loaded with product.

EDGE CONVEYOR 
Proper design of the edge conveying system is critical, 
as typically only 0.17 inches (4 mm) is in contact with 
the bottom side edges of the product. If the conveyor 
has lateral warpage of greater than this amount, the 
product will fall into the oven. Thus, edge conveyor 
straightness is a key issue in SMT processing. 
As the conveyor rails heat during the machine warm-up 
period, they will grow and tend to warp. The patented 
system from Research, Inc. shown below tensions the 
rails, which pulls the rail assembly straight. The lever 
(outlined in dark) is attached to the rail. The bottom side 
of the lever is attached to an adjustable spring mechanism 
that runs from end to end in the machine. Approximately 
1500 lbs (681 kg) of tensioning force is applied to each 
rail to maintain straightness. The machine frame is made 
of welded structural tubing in order to maintain its 
structural integrity. 
The use of the tensioning system allows the mass of the 
rails to be maintained at a reasonably low value, which 
minimizes the thermal affect of the rail on the product.

    45→HOW DO YOU ACHIEVE HIGH QUALITY SOLDER JOINTS? 
    46→The process of producing high quality solder joints is 
    47→similar to the process of learning how to ride a bicycle. 
    48→If you do not understand the fundamentals, it is virtually 
    49→impossible. However, once you understand and imple- 
    50→ment the basics, the results will follow. The goal of all 
    51→SMT process engineers is to repeatedly produce high 
    52→quality solder joints that have fine grain structure and 
    53→excellent wetting characteristics, as shown in the figure 
    54→below: 
    55→SURFACES MUST BE 
    56→CLEAN AND SOLDERABLE 
    57→II MUST BE 
    58→11 SMALL 
    59→CONTROL VARIABLES 
    60→In order to produce high quality solderjoints, all process 
    61→variables must be in control. The five general process 
    62→variables (l) that need to be in control include the mate- 
    63→rials, machines, manpower, methods, and the environ- 
    64→ment. If the process variables are not in control, there is 
    65→a very good chance that soldering defects will exist. 
    66→Let’s take a closer look at each. 
    67→MATERIALS 
    68→The materials must meet functional specifications so 
    69→that the product will perform to specification. Of equal 
    70→importance is the solderability of the assembly. The 
    71→solder paste/flux system must be compatible with the 
    72→base materials of the parts to be soldered. The solder 
    73→paste and parts should be as fresh as possible to enhance 
    74→solderability. 
    75→MACHINES 
    76→The machines used in the process must be able to perform 
    77→to their specifications. The machines should operate 
    78→within the range for which they are designed. Pushing a 
    79→machine beyond its operating limits will ultimately cause 
    80→a problem. The machines must be reliable and service- 
    81→able. 
    82→MANPOWER 
    83→The manpower must be properly trained. All machines in 
    84→the line require knowledgeable operators and mainte- 
    85→nance personnel. A machine is only as good as the person 
    86→operating it. 
    87→METHODS 
    88→The methods and procedures must be defined and strictly 
    89→adhered to. Inventory procedures should be implemented 
    90→to ensure that components and boards do not stay on the 
    91→shelf too long. Problems should be fully documented 
    92→including all data that pertains to it. 
    93→ENVIRONMENT 
    94→Finally, the processing environment must be controlled. 
    95→This includes both the environment inside and outside of 
    96→the machines. For example, if the humidity in the solder- 
    97→ing area is too high, this can cause the solder paste to 
    98→absorb moisture, whichmay cause problems duringreflow . 
    99→If the temperature in the room is not controlled, the 
   100→thermal profile in the reflow oven may be affected, which 
   101→again may cause a defect. 
   102→The purpose of this text is to address one aspect of high 
   103→quality SMT soldering, the reflow process. 
   104→Producing high quality solder joints 
   105→requires that five general process 
   106→variables need to be in control; the 
   107→materials, machines, manpower, 
   108→methods, and the environment.

   112→WHAT IS THE IMPORTANCE OF THE PROFILE? 
   113→I I I I I I 1; I :I I I I I 
   114→In order to fully understand Surface Mount Technology 
   115→(SMT) reflow, one needs to have an understanding of 
   116→what is being accomplished. One can take too simplistic 
   117→a viewpoint in that all you need to do is to heat solder 
   118→to a temperature greater than its melting point. One can 
   119→also take too complicated a viewpoint in believing that a 
   120→certain wavelength of infrared (IR) is required, or that a 
   121→certain percentage of convection is required. Perhaps the 
   122→most astute comment made on surface mount reflow was 
   123→by an individual whom had just completed an evaluation 
   124→of vapor phase, panel IR, and lamp IR equipment nearly 
   125→five years ago. After coming up with virtually identical 
   126→soldering defect results on all three types of soldering 
   127→equipment, the following comment was made: “If you 
   128→could hit the correct reflow profile using buckets of hot 
   129→water, you would accomplish high quality, low defect 
   130→solder joints.” Although the above comment was made 
   131→in jest (hot water is not quite hot enough to reflow solder), 
   132→there is considerable truth to what was said. 
   133→I 
   134→REFLOW PROFILE REQUIREMENT 
   135→High quality, low defect soldering requires identifying 
   136→the optimum temperature profile for reflowing the solder 
   137→paste, and repeating over and over. Every solder joint on 
   138→every board, needs to be heated similarily if the desired 
   139→soldering results are to be accomplished. It does not 
   140→matter how you apply the heat to the solder joint. What 
   141→does matter is that the heat is applied to the solder joint 
   142→in a controlled manner. The heating and cooling rise 
   143→rates must be compatible with the solder paste and 
   144→components. The amount of time that the assembly is 
   145→exposed to certain temperatures must be defined and 
   146→maintained. In other words, the solder reflow profile 
   147→must first be defined and then maintained.

   159→TYPICAL PROFILE 
   160→A typical profile consists of a preheat, dryout, and reflow 
   161→section (zone) where different heating rates are used. In 
   162→the preheat section, the goal is to fully preheat the SMT 
   163→assembly to temperatures generally between 100°C to 
   164→150°C. The most critical parameter in the preheat section 
   165→is to minimize the rate of rise to less than 2”C/second. 
   166→The main concern is minimizing thermal shock on the 
   167→components of the assembly. Multilayer ceramic chip 
   168→capacitors can be vulnerable to cracking if heated too 
   169→fast. Solder paste can spatter also, if heated too fast. 
   170→The second heating section, referred to as the dryout, 
   171→soak, or preflow zone, is used primarily to ensure that 
   172→the solder paste is fully dried before hitting reflow 
   173→temperatures. This zone also acts as a flux activation 
   174→zone for some solder pastes. Solder reflow is accom- 
   175→plished in the reflow zone, where the solder paste is 
   176→elevated to a temperature greater than the melting point 
   177→of the solder. For 63/37 Eutectic solder, the melting 
   178→temperature is 183°C. This temperature must be ex- 
   179→ceeded by approximately 20°C to ensure quality reflow. 
   180→The amount of time the solder joint is above the melting 
   181→point is referred to as the “wetting time”. The wetting 
   182→time is normally 30 to 60 seconds for most pastes. If the 
   183→wetting time is excessive, intermetallics may occur in 
   184→the joint, which result in brittle solder joints. In sum- 
   185→mary, define the profile, and hit it.

   243→WHAT IS THE PROFILE PROCESS BAND? 
   244→In reality the profile is not a line, but rather a band or 
   245→process window.(*) The size of the band is defined by the 
   246→range of temperature deviation that can occur during 
   247→reflow and yield high quality results. This is indicated 
   248→by the crosshatched area shown in the figure. In the 
   249→example, the profile band size is indicated as 25°C. 
   250→The actual size of the band will vary depending upon 
   251→solder paste, component type, and circuit board material.

   262→REFLOW SOLDERING DEFECTS 
   263→If the product temperature profile is not maintained 
   264→within the band, a defect will occur. Chip capacitors 
   265→may crack if the rise rate in the preheat zone is exces- 
   266→sive. Solder spatter and solder balls may occur if drying 
   267→is excessive or insufficient. If drying is excessive, the 
   268→solder paste may skin over and not allow any of the 
   269→volatiles to escape. As the temperature of the solder joint 
   270→continues to heat, the vapor pressure increases until the 
   271→solder joint virtually explodes as the gases escape rap- 
   272→idly. The result is solder spatter and solder balls. If the 
   273→preheat is insufficient, solder spatter and balls may occur 
   274→in the reflow zone when higher heating rates occur. It is 
   275→critical that the paste is dried at low controlled heating 
   276→rates. In the reflow zone, insufficient heat will result in 
   277→non-reflowed or partially reflowed solder joints. The 
   278→joints will have a dull, rough surface finish in this case. 
   279→Excessive heating in the reflow zone may result in burnt 
   280→boards, damaged components, or possibly solder 
   281→dewetting. In a dewet solder joint, the solder is reflowed 
   282→but it is pulled away from the pad or the component lead. 
   283→DEFINE THE BAND 
   284→The profile band needs to be defined for the given SMT 
   285→assembly. To define this band, one should be aware of 
   286→not only the solder paste requirements, but also any 
   287→specific requirements of components or the circuit board 
   288→material. The process band width is defined as the total 
   289→deviation in temperature that can occur and yield reliable 
   290→results. 
   291→OVEN PERFORMANCE 
   292→From a process standpoint, the reflow oven must be able 
   293→to produce consistent results within the reflow profile 
   294→band. The user should be aware of all variables that 
   295→influence the band. These variables may be defined as 
   296→product related and oven related. By far the most critical 
   297→product related non-uniformity is that created by large 
   298→mass differences on the product. Since it is easier to heat 
   299→an area that has no components as compared with an area 
   300→with large components, temperature differentials will 
   301→exist on the product. Machine related non-uniformities 
   302→such as repeatability under product load and edge-to- 
   303→center and front-to-back product heating uniformities 
   304→must also be considered. To achieve high quality, low 
   305→defect soldering results, the sum of all the non-uniformi- 
   306→ties must fall within the defined reflow profile band. 
   307→In reality the profile is not a line, but rather 
   308→a range of temperatures all solder joints 
   309→must be exposed. 
   310→The total temperature deviation from 
   311→component thermal mismatch, oven load- 
   312→ing, and oven uniformity must be within 
   313→the band.

   317→WHAT ARE THE CAUSES OF NON-UNIFORM HEATING? 
   318→In order to fully comprehend the capability to heat within 
   319→the defined process band, one needs to better understand 
   320→the causes of heating non-uniformities. The three main 
   321→causes of non-uniform heating in the SMT reflow pro- 
   322→cess include mass differential on the product, conveyor 
   323→and heater edge effects, and product loading. 
   324→MASS DIFFERENTIAL 
   325→The amount of temperature rise of a product as it travels 
   326→through a heating zone depends upon a number of 
   327→variables. The temperature rise of an object subjected to 
   328→heat is determined by the following equation:

   336→Cp = Specific Heat (w-sec/kg-”C) 
   337→The mass (M) times the specific heat (Cp) is often referred 
   338→to as thermal mass. Greater thermal mass requires more 
   339→heat to achieve a given temperature rise. In the figure

   394→WHAT ARE THE MODES OF HEATING? 
   395→There are three different heating modes involved wit 
   396→most SMT reflow processes; convection, conductior 
   397→and infrared radiation (IR). All three of these heatin

   399→easiest way to understand each of these heating mode

   453→Infrared (IR) heat transfer occurs when two objects at

   456→1000 micron wavelengths. All objects emit some level 
   457→of infrared. The quantity of infrared energy emitted and

   462→temperature results in shorter wavelengths. Decreasing 
   463→the source temperature results in longer wavelengths. In

   465→as not to exceed the 2OC/sec rate. When operating at

   598→In SMT reflow applications, there is no such thing as 
   599→pure convection or pure IR. The only way to achieve a 
   600→100% convection system would be to have gas flowing 
   601→over the product with no chamber walls. Of course this 
   602→in not practical. To have a 100% IR system, the chamber 
   603→would need to be operated in a vacuum. Again, this is not 
   604→the case. However, some systems are more dominated by 
   605→convection, while others utilize IR as the primary heat 
   606→source. For the sake of simplicity this text will refer to a 
   607→convection dominated machine as a convection ma- 
   608→chine, and an IR dominate machine as an IR machine. 
   609→CONVECTION 
   610→Both convection and IR have their unique advantages 
   611→and limitations. In convective systems, typically the 
   612→temperature of the flow is close to the desired tempera- 
   613→ture of the product in a given zone. This has the 
   614→advantage in that the product temperature will never 
   615→exceed the gas flow temperature. This is useful when 
   616→heating a product that has a large difference in the mass 
   617→of the components and distribution. In this case, the 
   618→larger components will continue to heat, while the smaller 
   619→components will not overheat. Convection heat transfer 
   620→is not thermally efficient. Air (or nitrogen) has a very low 
   621→heat capacity, which means that high volumes of flow 
   622→may be required to transfer the heat. One way to improve 
   623→efficiency and reduce the amount of process gas required

   669→WHAT ARE THE BENEFITS OF A NITROGEN ATMOSPHERE? 
   670→~ 
   671→Ease of cleaning flux 
   672→residues (RMA) 
   673→Reflow soldering in a nitrogen atmosphere is becoming 
   674→a significant process consideration. The issue is really 
   675→not the ability to reflow in nitrogen, but rather the ability 
   676→to reflow in the absence of oxygen. Heating solder in 
   677→the presence of oxygen will create oxides, which are 
   678→generally non-solderable surfaces. In past days of reflow 
   679→soldering, the solder paste consisted of aggressive enough 
   680→fluxes to remove oxides during the reflow process. The 
   681→future trend is moving away from strong fluxes in the 
   682→paste. The future trends include two major process 
   683→changes that are driving the need for reflow in nitrogen 
   684→atmospheres; fine pitch soldering and no-clean fluxes. 
   685→500 ppm 
   686→FINE PITCH REFLOW SOLDERING 
   687→Fine pitch soldering presents many challenges. In order 
   688→to obtain satisfactory paste print definition, the particle 
   689→sizes of tin and lead are becoming smaller. As the 
   690→particles become smaller, the ratio of surface area to 
   691→volume of the particles increases. This can be shown by: 
   692→RATIO = (n x D*) /(1/6 x n x D3) 
   693→RATIO = 6 / D 
   694→WHERE: 
   695→D = Particle Diameter 
   696→FOR THE SAME VOLUME (OR MASS) OF SOLDER, THERE IS 
   697→GREATER SURFACE AREA WITH SMALLER PARTICLES THAN 
   698→WITH LARGER PARTICLES. 
   699→Thus, as particles sizes decrease, the ratio increases. 
   700→With more available surface area in the solder paste, 
   701→there is a greater tendency towards oxidation. Keep in 
   702→mind that oxidation is a function of the metals involved, 
   703→the temperatures of the metal, the exposed surface area, 
   704→and the amount of oxygen present. The only variable 
   705→that one can control is the amount of oxygen present. 
   706→This can only be done through proper oven design. 
   707→NO-CLEAN SOLDERING 
   708→The second technology change that is driving the need 
   709→towards nitrogen atmospheres is the greater usage of no- 
   710→clean pastes. The rapid trend away from solvent cleaning 
   711→is creating this and other needs. No-clean soldering 
   712→requires a tight control of the process. All of the compo- 
   713→nents and boards must be highly solderable. The reflow 
   714→process must not add any significant oxidation to the 
   715→process. The fluxes used are very weak, and do not have 
   716→aggressive oxide cleaning action. In addition, there is no 
   717→cleaning that would remove any solder balls from the 
   718→product. These solder balls eventually can create short 
   719→circuits on the product if they are not removed. Reflowing 
   720→in a high purity nitrogen environment reduces the possi- 
   721→bility of creating solder balls. 
   722→A good question to ask is “How pure a nitrogen environ- 
   723→ment is required?” A recent study (4) by Colin Lea of the 
   724→National Physics Laboratory in the United Kingdom was 
   725→conducted to determine the affect of nitrogen purity on 
   726→the process. The conclusions drawn in the study are 
   727→listed below: 
   728→DESCRIPTION I PURITY LEVEL I 
   729→Significant reduction 
   730→in board discoloration 
   731→10,000 ppm 
   732→Reduction in solder 200 ppm 
   733→balling (RMA) 
   734→Reflow of low-residue 
   735→solder paste 
   736→< 100 ppm 
   737→The paper presents a number of excellent graphs that 
   738→show the affect of nitrogen purity on parameters includ- 
   739→ing flux spread, wetting force, wetting time, solder balls, 
   740→cleaning, residue, board discoloration, and micro-struc- 
   741→ture. It is recommended reading if your process may 
   742→require the use of nitrogen. You must determine the 
   743→nitrogen requirements for your process. The benefits of 
   744→using nitrogen definitely exist, however you must deter- 
   745→mine if the additional cost of nitrogen is worthwhile for 
   746→your process.

   751→WHAT ARE THE STEPS IN THE SELECTION PROCESS? 
   752→When selecting reflow equipment, it is important to take 
   753→into consideration all aspects that may affect the process 
   754→and production. Try to avoid becoming too focussed on 
   755→one issue, such as populated uniformity, as it may not 
   756→lead you to the optimum decision. The recommended 
   757→steps in the selection process are described in the follow- 
   758→ing paragraphs. 
   759→DEFINE PROCESS BAND WIDTH 
   760→The first step is to define the acceptable process profile 
   761→band width for your SMT assemblies. Try to be as 
   762→accurate as possible when defining the band. If the band 
   763→is too restrictive, some aspect of production will be 
   764→negatively affected. If the band is too loose, a defect will 
   765→show up in the process. The band width should be 
   766→defined as a range of temperatures ("C) that the entire 
   767→profile must fall within. Refer to page 4 for a more 
   768→detailed description. 
   769→DEFINE HEATING NON-UNIFORMITIES 
   770→The next step is to define causes of heating non-unifor- 
   771→mities that may occur in the process. These non-unifor- 
   772→mities are caused by mass differential, oven uniformity, 
   773→and oven repeatability under production loading condi- 
   774→tions. A set of tests must be conducted with the desired 
   775→product on the oven in question. The sum of the non- 
   776→uniformities ("C) must be less than the profile band width 
   777→defined in the first step. Refer to page 5 for a more 
   778→detailed description. 
   779→SIZE THE OVEN PROPERLY 
   780→The oven must be sized to handle the production rate of 
   781→the pick-and-place equipment. The calculation is shown 
   782→below: 
   783→LINE SPEED - BOARDS PER MINUTE X LENGTH PER BOARD 
   784→(MINIMUM) - LOAD FACTOR 
   785→Operating at a conveyor speed greater than the calculated 
   786→speed ensures that no product jams will occur on the 
   787→onload area of the reflow oven. 
   788→Try to avoid becoming too focussed on one 
   789→issue, such as populated uniformity, as it may 
   790→not lead you to the optimum decision. 
   791→In order for the oven to be properly sized, the process

   799→DEFINE PROCESS GAS 
   800→If a nitrogen atmosphere is required for solderability or 
   801→no-clean processing (see page lo), one needs to consider 
   802→the purity required and the gas consumption. Be careful 
   803→how the purity is measured, such that it is not measured 
   804→at the gas inlet. 
   805→REVIEW CONVEYOR DESIGN 
   806→The conveying mechanism is perhaps the most over- 
   807→looked aspect of equipment selection. One needs to 
   808→define whether a mesh conveyor or an edge type is 
   809→required. Typically edge conveyors are used for in-line 
   810→processing or if double-sided assembly is required. The 
   811→most important issue with edge conveyors is the ability 
   812→for the conveyor to remain straight to avoid dropping 
   813→product. 
   814→RELIABILITY/SERVICEABILITY 
   815→Once a machine is placed into service, it is critical that it 
   816→remains operational. Evaluate the product design from a 
   817→structural as well as a functional standpoint. Is the oven 
   818→designed to withstand the rigors of production? Review 
   819→the product manuals, drawings, and spare parts lists. 
   820→Find out where the nearest servicing center is located. Is 
   821→training available? These are the questions that must be 
   822→asked during the selection process. 
   823→INTERFACING REQUIREMENTS 
   824→Conveyor and control interfacing requirements may also 
   825→be an important selection issue. Make sure that the edge 
   826→conveyor fixed rail justification is the same as the pick- 
   827→and-place equipment. Ask questions about networking 
   828→machines to a host and product flow control schemes if 
   829→needed.

  1052→One of the key oven performance issues is the ability to

  1059→LAMP DEFINITION 
  1060→The closed loop heat flux control method used in a 
  1061→Research, Inc. lamp based oven will be used as an 
  1062→example of one type of control. The primary heat source 
  1063→in this system is the tungsten filament (T3) lamp. The T3 
  1064→lamp consists of a tungsten filament encased in a sealed 
  1065→quartz envelope. The envelope is filled with an inert gas 
  1066→to keep the filament from oxidizing and failing. The 
  1067→lamps are rated for 5000 hours when operated at 100% 
  1068→capacity. In SMT applications, the lamp power never 
  1069→exceeds 20% capacity, resulting in lamp life in excess of 
  1070→20,000 hours. At typical operating setpoints of 5-15%,

  1074→The greatest advantage that T3 lamps have is their rapid

  1076→change occurs, the lamp is at its new temperature equi- 
  1077→librium. This rapid response is ideal for closed loop 
  1078→control, as energy can be replaced in the heating chamber 
  1079→instantly after its removal.

HOW DO YOU ACHIEVE HIGH QUALITY SOLDER JOINTS? 
The process of producing high quality solder joints is 
similar to the process of learning how to ride a bicycle. 
If you do not understand the fundamentals, it is virtually 
impossible. However, once you understand and imple- 
ment the basics, the results will follow. The goal of all 
SMT process engineers is to repeatedly produce high 
quality solder joints that have fine grain structure and 
excellent wetting characteristics, as shown in the figure 
below: 
SURFACES MUST BE 
CLEAN AND SOLDERABLE 
II MUST BE 
11 SMALL 
CONTROL VARIABLES 
In order to produce high quality solderjoints, all process 
variables must be in control. The five general process 
variables (l) that need to be in control include the mate- 
rials, machines, manpower, methods, and the environ- 
ment. If the process variables are not in control, there is 
a very good chance that soldering defects will exist. 
Let’s take a closer look at each. 
MATERIALS 
The materials must meet functional specifications so 
that the product will perform to specification. Of equal 
importance is the solderability of the assembly. The 
solder paste/flux system must be compatible with the 
base materials of the parts to be soldered. The solder 
paste and parts should be as fresh as possible to enhance 
solderability. 
MACHINES 
The machines used in the process must be able to perform 
to their specifications. The machines should operate 
within the range for which they are designed. Pushing a 
machine beyond its operating limits will ultimately cause 
a problem. The machines must be reliable and service- 
able. 
MANPOWER 
The manpower must be properly trained. All machines in 
the line require knowledgeable operators and mainte- 
nance personnel. A machine is only as good as the person 
operating it. 
METHODS 
The methods and procedures must be defined and strictly 
adhered to. Inventory procedures should be implemented 
to ensure that components and boards do not stay on the 
shelf too long. Problems should be fully documented 
including all data that pertains to it. 
ENVIRONMENT 
Finally, the processing environment must be controlled. 
This includes both the environment inside and outside of 
the machines. For example, if the humidity in the solder- 
ing area is too high, this can cause the solder paste to 
absorb moisture, whichmay cause problems duringreflow . 
If the temperature in the room is not controlled, the 
thermal profile in the reflow oven may be affected, which 
again may cause a defect. 
The purpose of this text is to address one aspect of high 
quality SMT soldering, the reflow process. 
Producing high quality solder joints 
requires that five general process 
variables need to be in control; the 
materials, machines, manpower, 
methods, and the environment. 
2 Section I - Technology 

=== Page 5 ===
WHAT IS THE IMPORTANCE OF THE PROFILE? 
I I I I I I 1; I :I I I I I 
In order to fully understand Surface Mount Technology 
(SMT) reflow, one needs to have an understanding of 
what is being accomplished. One can take too simplistic 
a viewpoint in that all you need to do is to heat solder 
to a temperature greater than its melting point. One can 
also take too complicated a viewpoint in believing that a 
certain wavelength of infrared (IR) is required, or that a 
certain percentage of convection is required. Perhaps the 
most astute comment made on surface mount reflow was 
by an individual whom had just completed an evaluation 
of vapor phase, panel IR, and lamp IR equipment nearly 
five years ago. After coming up with virtually identical 
soldering defect results on all three types of soldering 
equipment, the following comment was made: “If you 
could hit the correct reflow profile using buckets of hot 
water, you would accomplish high quality, low defect 
solder joints.” Although the above comment was made 
in jest (hot water is not quite hot enough to reflow solder), 
there is considerable truth to what was said. 
I 
REFLOW PROFILE REQUIREMENT 
High quality, low defect soldering requires identifying 
the optimum temperature profile for reflowing the solder 
paste, and repeating over and over. Every solder joint on 
every board, needs to be heated similarily if the desired 
soldering results are to be accomplished. It does not 
matter how you apply the heat to the solder joint. What 
does matter is that the heat is applied to the solder joint 
in a controlled manner. The heating and cooling rise 
rates must be compatible with the solder paste and 
components. The amount of time that the assembly is 
exposed to certain temperatures must be defined and 
maintained. In other words, the solder reflow profile 
must first be defined and then maintained. 
280- 
260-

High quality, low defect soldering 
requires identifying the optimum 
temperature profile for reflowing 
the solder paste, and repeating it 
over and over. 
I WETTING ; ‘ TIME , 
30-60 .’ : SEC ~ 
TYPICAL PROFILE 
A typical profile consists of a preheat, dryout, and reflow 
section (zone) where different heating rates are used. In 
the preheat section, the goal is to fully preheat the SMT 
assembly to temperatures generally between 100°C to 
150°C. The most critical parameter in the preheat section 
is to minimize the rate of rise to less than 2”C/second. 
The main concern is minimizing thermal shock on the 
components of the assembly. Multilayer ceramic chip 
capacitors can be vulnerable to cracking if heated too 
fast. Solder paste can spatter also, if heated too fast. 
The second heating section, referred to as the dryout, 
soak, or preflow zone, is used primarily to ensure that 
the solder paste is fully dried before hitting reflow 
temperatures. This zone also acts as a flux activation 
zone for some solder pastes. Solder reflow is accom- 
plished in the reflow zone, where the solder paste is 
elevated to a temperature greater than the melting point 
of the solder. For 63/37 Eutectic solder, the melting 
temperature is 183°C. This temperature must be ex- 
ceeded by approximately 20°C to ensure quality reflow. 
The amount of time the solder joint is above the melting 
point is referred to as the “wetting time”. The wetting 
time is normally 30 to 60 seconds for most pastes. If the 
wetting time is excessive, intermetallics may occur in 
the joint, which result in brittle solder joints. In sum- 
mary, define the profile, and hit it. 
Section I - Technology 3 

=== Page 6 ===
HOW MANY HEATING ZONES ARE REQUIRED? 
This question frequently arrives and can be a source of 
confusion. One theory is that if ten zones are good, then

non-reflowed or partially reflowed solder joints. The

but it is pulled away from the pad or the component lead.

Fine pitch soldering presents many challenges. In order

The second technology change that is driving the need 
towards nitrogen atmospheres is the greater usage of no- 
clean pastes. The rapid trend away from solvent cleaning

show up in the process. The band width should be 
defined as a range of temperatures ("C) that the entire 
profile must fall within. Refer to page 4 for a more 
detailed description.

mities that may occur in the process. These non-unifor- 
mities are caused by mass differential, oven uniformity,

tions. A set of tests must be conducted with the desired

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""
Reflow Machine Analysis Script
Processes thermocouple data, MES logs, and defect data to answer compliance questions
"""

import pandas as pd
import json
import os
from collections import defaultdict

# Create output directory
os.makedirs('/app/output', exist_ok=True)

# Load data
print("Loading data files...")
mes_log = pd.read_csv('/app/data/mes_log.csv')
thermocouples = pd.read_csv('/app/data/thermocouples.csv')
test_defects = pd.read_csv('/app/data/test_defects.csv')

print(f"MES log: {len(mes_log)} rows")
print(f"Thermocouples: {len(thermocouples)} rows")
print(f"Test defects: {len(test_defects)} rows")

# ==============================================================================
# QUESTION 1: Maximum Temperature Ramp Rate During Preheat
# ==============================================================================
print("\n" + "="*80)
print("QUESTION 1: Maximum Temperature Ramp Rate During Preheat")
print("="*80)

# From handbook Page 5, lines 160-169:
# - Preheat section: temperatures generally between 100°C to 150°C
# - Critical parameter: minimize rate of rise to LESS THAN 2°C/second
PREHEAT_TEMP_MIN = 100  # °C
PREHEAT_TEMP_MAX = 150  # °C
RAMP_RATE_LIMIT = 2.0   # °C/s

print(f"Preheat region: {PREHEAT_TEMP_MIN}°C to {PREHEAT_TEMP_MAX}°C")
print(f"Ramp rate limit: {RAMP_RATE_LIMIT}°C/s")

# Calculate ramp rates for each run
q1_results = {}
violating_runs = []

# Group by run_id and tc_id
for run_id in thermocouples['run_id'].unique():
    run_data = thermocouples[thermocouples['run_id'] == run_id]

    # Get unique tc_ids for this run
    tc_ids = run_data['tc_id'].unique()

    max_ramp_per_tc = {}

    for tc_id in tc_ids:
        tc_data = run_data[run_data['tc_id'] == tc_id].sort_values('time_s')

        # Filter data in preheat region (100-150°C)
        preheat_data = tc_data[(tc_data['temp_c'] >= PREHEAT_TEMP_MIN) &
                               (tc_data['temp_c'] <= PREHEAT_TEMP_MAX)]

        if len(preheat_data) < 2:
            continue

        # Calculate ramp rates between consecutive points
        max_ramp = 0
        for i in range(len(preheat_data) - 1):
            dt = preheat_data.iloc[i+1]['time_s'] - preheat_data.iloc[i]['time_s']
            dtemp = preheat_data.iloc[i+1]['temp_c'] - preheat_data.iloc[i]['temp_c']
            if dt > 0:
                ramp_rate = dtemp / dt
                max_ramp = max(max_ramp, ramp_rate)

        max_ramp_per_tc[tc_id] = round(max_ramp, 2)

    # Select TC1 (largest_mass) as the most representative based on handbook guidance
    # The handbook mentions measuring thermal mass differential on largest device
    if 'TC1' in max_ramp_per_tc:
        selected_tc = 'TC1'
        max_preheat_ramp = max_ramp_per_tc['TC1']
    elif max_ramp_per_tc:
        # If TC1 doesn't exist, use the first available
        selected_tc = list(max_ramp_per_tc.keys())[0]
        max_preheat_ramp = max_ramp_per_tc[selected_tc]
    else:
        selected_tc = None
        max_preheat_ramp = None

    if max_preheat_ramp is not None:
        q1_results[run_id] = {
            "tc_id": selected_tc,
            "max_preheat_ramp_c_per_s": max_preheat_ramp
        }

        if max_preheat_ramp > RAMP_RATE_LIMIT:
            violating_runs.append(run_id)

# Sort results
q1_results = dict(sorted(q1_results.items()))
violating_runs = sorted(violating_runs)

q1_output = {
    "ramp_rate_limit_c_per_s": RAMP_RATE_LIMIT,
    "violating_runs": violating_runs,
    "max_ramp_by_run": q1_results
}

with open('/app/output/q01.json', 'w') as f:
    json.dump(q1_output, f, indent=2)

print(f"Processed {len(q1_results)} runs")
print(f"Violating runs: {len(violating_runs)}")
print(f"Output saved to /app/output/q01.json")

# ==============================================================================
# QUESTION 2: Time Above Liquidus (TAL)
# ==============================================================================
print("\n" + "="*80)
print("QUESTION 2: Time Above Liquidus (TAL)")
print("="*80)

# From handbook Page 5, lines 177-183:
# - Wetting time: 30 to 60 seconds (time above melting point)
# - For 63/37 Eutectic solder, melting temperature is 183°C
TAL_MIN = 30  # seconds
TAL_MAX = 60  # seconds

print(f"TAL window: {TAL_MIN}s to {TAL_MAX}s")

q2_results = []

# Get liquidus temperature for each run from MES log
for run_id in sorted(thermocouples['run_id'].unique()):
    run_mes = mes_log[mes_log['run_id'] == run_id]
    if len(run_mes) == 0:
        continue

    liquidus_temp = run_mes.iloc[0]['solder_liquidus_c']

    run_data = thermocouples[thermocouples['run_id'] == run_id]

    # Use TC1 (largest_mass) as representative
    tc1_data = run_data[run_data['tc_id'] == 'TC1'].sort_values('time_s')

    if len(tc1_data) == 0:
        # If TC1 doesn't exist, skip
        continue

    # Calculate time above liquidus
    above_liquidus = tc1_data[tc1_data['temp_c'] > liquidus_temp]

    if len(above_liquidus) > 0:
        tal_s = above_liquidus['time_s'].max() - above_liquidus['time_s'].min()
    else:
        tal_s = 0.0

    tal_s = round(tal_s, 2)

    # Check compliance
    if TAL_MIN <= tal_s <= TAL_MAX:

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""
Reflow Machine Analysis Script
Processes thermocouple data, MES logs, and defect data to answer compliance questions
"""

import pandas as pd
import json
import os
from collections import defaultdict

# Create output directory
os.makedirs('/app/output', exist_ok=True)

# Load data
print("Loading data files...")
mes_log = pd.read_csv('/app/data/mes_log.csv')
thermocouples = pd.read_csv('/app/data/thermocouples.csv')
test_defects = pd.read_csv('/app/data/test_defects.csv')

print(f"MES log: {len(mes_log)} rows")
print(f"Thermocouples: {len(thermocouples)} rows")
print(f"Test defects: {len(test_defects)} rows")

# ==============================================================================
# QUESTION 1: Maximum Temperature Ramp Rate During Preheat
# ==============================================================================
print("\n" + "="*80)
print("QUESTION 1: Maximum Temperature Ramp Rate During Preheat")
print("="*80)

# From handbook Page 5, lines 160-169:
# - Preheat section: temperatures generally between 100°C to 150°C
# - Critical parameter: minimize rate of rise to LESS THAN 2°C/second
PREHEAT_TEMP_MIN = 100  # °C
PREHEAT_TEMP_MAX = 150  # °C
RAMP_RATE_LIMIT = 2.0   # °C/s

print(f"Preheat region: {PREHEAT_TEMP_MIN}°C to {PREHEAT_TEMP_MAX}°C")
print(f"Ramp rate limit: {RAMP_RATE_LIMIT}°C/s")

# Calculate ramp rates for each run
q1_results = {}
violating_runs = []

# Group by run_id and tc_id
for run_id in thermocouples['run_id'].unique():
    run_data = thermocouples[thermocouples['run_id'] == run_id]

    # Get unique tc_ids for this run
    tc_ids = run_data['tc_id'].unique()

    max_ramp_per_tc = {}

    for tc_id in tc_ids:
        tc_data = run_data[run_data['tc_id'] == tc_id].sort_values('time_s')

        # Filter data in preheat region (100-150°C)
        preheat_data = tc_data[(tc_data['temp_c'] >= PREHEAT_TEMP_MIN) &
                               (tc_data['temp_c'] <= PREHEAT_TEMP_MAX)]

        if len(preheat_data) < 2:
            continue

        # Calculate ramp rates between consecutive points
        max_ramp = 0
        for i in range(len(preheat_data) - 1):
            dt = preheat_data.iloc[i+1]['time_s'] - preheat_data.iloc[i]['time_s']
            dtemp = preheat_data.iloc[i+1]['temp_c'] - preheat_data.iloc[i]['temp_c']
            if dt > 0:
                ramp_rate = dtemp / dt
                max_ramp = max(max_ramp, ramp_rate)

        max_ramp_per_tc[tc_id] = round(max_ramp, 2)

    # Select TC1 (largest_mass) as the most representative based on handbook guidance
    # The handbook mentions measuring thermal mass differential on largest device
    if 'TC1' in max_ramp_per_tc:
        selected_tc = 'TC1'
        max_preheat_ramp = max_ramp_per_tc['TC1']
    elif max_ramp_per_tc:
        # If TC1 doesn't exist, use the first available
        selected_tc = list(max_ramp_per_tc.keys())[0]
        max_preheat_ramp = max_ramp_per_tc[selected_tc]
    else:
        selected_tc = None
        max_preheat_ramp = None

    if max_preheat_ramp is not None:
        q1_results[run_id] = {
            "tc_id": selected_tc,
            "max_preheat_ramp_c_per_s": max_preheat_ramp
        }

        if max_preheat_ramp > RAMP_RATE_LIMIT:
            violating_runs.append(run_id)

# Sort results
q1_results = dict(sorted(q1_results.items()))
violating_runs = sorted(violating_runs)

q1_output = {
    "ramp_rate_limit_c_per_s": RAMP_RATE_LIMIT,
    "violating_runs": violating_runs,
    "max_ramp_by_run": q1_results
}

with open('/app/output/q01.json', 'w') as f:
    json.dump(q1_output, f, indent=2)

print(f"Processed {len(q1_results)} runs")
print(f"Violating runs: {len(violating_runs)}")
print(f"Output saved to /app/output/q01.json")

# ==============================================================================
# QUESTION 2: Time Above Liquidus (TAL)
# ==============================================================================
print("\n" + "="*80)
print("QUESTION 2: Time Above Liquidus (TAL)")
print("="*80)

# From handbook Page 5, lines 177-183:
# - Wetting time: 30 to 60 seconds (time above melting point)
# - For 63/37 Eutectic solder, melting temperature is 183°C
TAL_MIN = 30  # seconds
TAL_MAX = 60  # seconds

print(f"TAL window: {TAL_MIN}s to {TAL_MAX}s")

q2_results = []

# Get liquidus temperature for each run from MES log
for run_id in sorted(thermocouples['run_id'].unique()):
    run_mes = mes_log[mes_log['run_id'] == run_id]
    if len(run_mes) == 0:
        continue

    liquidus_temp = run_mes.iloc[0]['solder_liquidus_c']

    run_data = thermocouples[thermocouples['run_id'] == run_id]

    # Use TC1 (largest_mass) as representative
    tc1_data = run_data[run_data['tc_id'] == 'TC1'].sort_values('time_s')

    if len(tc1_data) == 0:
        # If TC1 doesn't exist, skip
        continue

    # Calculate time above liquidus
    above_liquidus = tc1_data[tc1_data['temp_c'] > liquidus_temp]

    if len(above_liquidus) > 0:
        tal_s = above_liquidus['time_s'].max() - above_liquidus['time_s'].min()
    else:
        tal_s = 0.0

    tal_s = round(tal_s, 2)

    # Check compliance
    if TAL_MIN <= tal_s <= TAL_MAX:
        status = "compliant"
    else:
        status = "non-compliant"

    q2_results.append({
        "run_id": run_id,
        "tc_id": "TC1",
        "tal_s": tal_s,
        "required_min_tal_s": TAL_MIN,
        "required_max_tal_s": TAL_MAX,
        "status": status
    })

with open('/app/output/q02.json', 'w') as f:
    json.dump(q2_results, f, indent=2)

print(f"Processed {len(q2_results)} runs")
print(f"Output saved to /app/output/q02.json")

# ==============================================================================
# QUESTION 3: Peak Temperature Requirements
# ==============================================================================
print("\n" + "="*80)
print("QUESTION 3: Peak Temperature Requirements")
print("="*80)

# From handbook Page 5, lines 176-179:
# - Temperature must exceed melting point by approximately 20°C to ensure quality reflow
# - For 63/37 Eutectic, melting is 183°C, so minimum peak = 183 + 20 = 203°C

q3_results = {}
failing_runs = []

for run_id in sorted(mes_log['run_id'].unique()):
    run_mes = mes_log[mes_log['run_id'] == run_id]
    liquidus_temp = run_mes.iloc[0]['solder_liquidus_c']

    # Minimum peak = liquidus + 20°C
    required_min_peak = liquidus_temp + 20

    run_data = thermocouples[thermocouples['run_id'] == run_id]

    if len(run_data) == 0:
        # No thermocouple data - run is failing
        failing_runs.append(run_id)
        q3_results[run_id] = {
            "tc_id": None,
            "peak_temp_c": None,
            "required_min_peak_c": round(required_min_peak, 2)
        }
        continue

    # Use TC1 (largest_mass) as representative
    tc1_data = run_data[run_data['tc_id'] == 'TC1']

    if len(tc1_data) == 0:
        # No TC1 data
        failing_runs.append(run_id)
        q3_results[run_id] = {
            "tc_id": None,
            "peak_temp_c": None,
            "required_min_peak_c": round(required_min_peak, 2)
        }
        continue

    peak_temp = tc1_data['temp_c'].max()
    peak_temp = round(peak_temp, 2)

    q3_results[run_id] = {
        "tc_id": "TC1",
        "peak_temp_c": peak_temp,
        "required_min_peak_c": round(required_min_peak, 2)
    }

    if peak_temp < required_min_peak:
        failing_runs.append(run_id)

q3_output = {
    "failing_runs": sorted(failing_runs),
    "min_peak_by_run": q3_results
}

with open('/app/output/q03.json', 'w') as f:
    json.dump(q3_output, f, indent=2)

print(f"Processed {len(q3_results)} runs")
print(f"Failing runs: {len(failing_runs)}")
print(f"Output saved to /app/output/q03.json")

# ==============================================================================
# QUESTION 4: Conveyor Speed Feasibility
# ==============================================================================
print("\n" + "="*80)
print("QUESTION 4: Conveyor Speed Feasibility")
print("="*80)

# From handbook, we need to check thermal dwell requirements
# The process dwell time must allow proper heating through all zones
# Minimum speed calculation from Page 14, lines 783-798:
# LINE SPEED (MINIMUM) = BOARDS PER MINUTE × LENGTH PER BOARD / LOAD FACTOR
# PROCESS SPEED = OVEN CHAMBER HEATED LENGTH / PROCESS DWELL TIME

# We need to infer the required minimum speed from the thermal profile requirements
# The process must allow sufficient dwell time for proper reflow

q4_results = []

for idx, row in mes_log.iterrows():
    run_id = row['run_id']
    actual_speed = row['conveyor_speed_cm_min']
    board_length = row['board_length_cm']

    # Get thermocouple data to determine actual dwell time
    run_data = thermocouples[thermocouples['run_id'] == run_id]

    if len(run_data) > 0:
        # Total dwell time = max time in oven
        total_dwell_s = run_data['time_s'].max()

        # For proper reflow, we need:
        # - Time to reach preheat temp (100-150°C)
        # - Dryout/soak time
        # - Time above liquidus (30-60s)
        # - Cooling time
        # Typical total process time is 3-6 minutes based on industry standards

        # The required minimum speed ensures the board doesn't move too fast
        # Speed = Distance / Time
        # If board moves too fast, insufficient heating occurs

        # Based on the profile, minimum dwell should be ~180 seconds for proper reflow
        # This comes from: preheat (60s) + dryout (60s) + reflow (60s) minimum
        required_min_dwell_s = 180

        # But we should use actual achieved dwell if it worked
        # The actual speed already achieved this dwell, so it's the minimum
        # required_min_speed = (board_length / total_dwell_s) * 60  # cm/min

        # Actually, the constraint is that conveyor speed must be slow enough
        # to allow proper thermal dwell. So minimum speed is zero, and there's
        # a MAXIMUM speed constraint

        # Let me re-read the handbook requirement...
        # The requirement is about sizing the oven to avoid bottlenecks
        # But for thermal compliance, speed must be slow enough for proper heating

        # Without explicit constraints in handbook about max speed,
        # I'll use the requirement that total dwell must be >= 180s for complete profile
        required_min_speed = (board_length / required_min_dwell_s) * 60
    else:
        # No thermocouple data - cannot determine requirement
        required_min_speed = None

    meets = True
    if required_min_speed is not None and actual_speed is not None:
        # Speed must be >= minimum (fast enough to avoid jams)
        # but also slow enough for thermal dwell
        # Since we calculated min speed from required dwell,
        # actual speed should be <= max allowed for proper heating

        # Actually, let me reconsider: the question asks if speed is "feasible"
        # Feasible means it allows proper processing
        # Too fast = insufficient heating
        # Too slow = OK but inefficient

        # Calculate maximum allowable speed for minimum required dwell
        max_allowable_speed = (board_length / required_min_dwell_s) * 60

        if actual_speed > max_allowable_speed:
            meets = False

        required_min_speed = round(max_allowable_speed, 2)
    elif actual_speed is None:
        meets = False
        required_min_speed = None

    q4_results.append({
        "run_id": run_id,
        "required_min_speed_cm_min": required_min_speed,
        "actual_speed_cm_min": round(actual_speed, 2) if actual_speed is not None else None,
        "meets": meets
    })

# Sort by run_id
q4_results = sorted(q4_results, key=lambda x: x['run_id'])

with open('/app/output/q04.json', 'w') as f:
    json.dump(q4_results, f, indent=2)

print(f"Processed {len(q4_results)} runs")
print(f"Output saved to /app/output/q04.json")

# ==============================================================================
# QUESTION 5: Best Run Per Board Family
# ==============================================================================
print("\n" + "="*80)
print("QUESTION 5: Best Run Per Board Family")
print("="*80)

# Criteria for best run:
# 1. Quality: highest yield, fewest defects
# 2. Efficiency: fastest speed while meeting requirements
# 3. Compliance: meets all thermal requirements

# Load all previous results
with open('/app/output/q01.json', 'r') as f:
    q1_data = json.load(f)
with open('/app/output/q02.json', 'r') as f:
    q2_data = json.load(f)
with open('/app/output/q03.json', 'r') as f:
    q3_data = json.load(f)

# Create compliance lookup
q1_compliant = set([r for r in q1_data['max_ramp_by_run'].keys()
                    if r not in q1_data['violating_runs']])
q2_compliant = set([r['run_id'] for r in q2_data if r['status'] == 'compliant'])
q3_compliant = set([r for r in q3_data['min_peak_by_run'].keys()
                    if r not in q3_data['failing_runs']])

# Get yield data
yield_data = test_defects[test_defects['inspection_stage'] == 'SUMMARY']
yield_lookup = {}
for idx, row in yield_data.iterrows():
    yield_lookup[row['run_id']] = row['fp_yield_pct']

# Rank runs by board family
q5_results = []
board_families = mes_log['board_family'].unique()

for board_family in sorted(board_families):
    family_runs = mes_log[mes_log['board_family'] == board_family]['run_id'].tolist()

    # Score each run
    run_scores = []
    for run_id in family_runs:
        score = 0

        # Compliance checks (most important)
        compliant = (run_id in q1_compliant and
                    run_id in q2_compliant and
                    run_id in q3_compliant)

        if not compliant:
            # Non-compliant runs get negative score
            score -= 1000

        # Quality: yield percentage
        if run_id in yield_lookup:
            score += yield_lookup[run_id]

        # Efficiency: conveyor speed (higher is better for throughput)
        run_mes = mes_log[mes_log['run_id'] == run_id].iloc[0]
        speed = run_mes['conveyor_speed_cm_min']
        score += speed / 10  # Normalized contribution

        run_scores.append((run_id, score))

    # Sort by score (descending)
    run_scores.sort(key=lambda x: x[1], reverse=True)

    if len(run_scores) > 0:
        best_run = run_scores[0][0]
        runner_ups = [r[0] for r in run_scores[1:]]
    else:
        best_run = None
        runner_ups = []

    q5_results.append({
        "board_family": board_family,
        "best_run_id": best_run,
        "runner_up_run_ids": runner_ups
    })

# Sort by board_family
q5_results = sorted(q5_results, key=lambda x: x['board_family'])

with open('/app/output/q05.json', 'w') as f:
    json.dump(q5_results, f, indent=2)

print(f"Processed {len(q5_results)} board families")
print(f"Output saved to /app/output/q05.json")

print("\n" + "="*80)
print("ALL ANALYSES COMPLETE")
print("="*80)

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""
Reflow Machine Analysis Script
Processes thermocouple data, MES logs, and defect data to answer compliance questions
"""

import pandas as pd
import json
import os
import numpy as np
from collections import defaultdict

# Custom JSON encoder to handle numpy types
class NumpyEncoder(json.JSONEncoder):
    def default(self, obj):
        if isinstance(obj, (np.integer, np.int64)):
            return int(obj)
        if isinstance(obj, (np.floating, np.float64)):
            return float(obj)
        if isinstance(obj, np.ndarray):
            return obj.tolist()
        return super().default(obj)

# Create output directory
os.makedirs('/app/output', exist_ok=True)

# Load data
print("Loading data files...")
mes_log = pd.read_csv('/app/data/mes_log.csv')
thermocouples = pd.read_csv('/app/data/thermocouples.csv')
test_defects = pd.read_csv('/app/data/test_defects.csv')

print(f"MES log: {len(mes_log)} rows")
print(f"Thermocouples: {len(thermocouples)} rows")
print(f"Test defects: {len(test_defects)} rows")

# ==============================================================================
# QUESTION 1: Maximum Temperature Ramp Rate During Preheat
# ==============================================================================
print("\n" + "="*80)
print("QUESTION 1: Maximum Temperature Ramp Rate During Preheat")
print("="*80)

# From handbook Page 5, lines 160-169:
# - Preheat section: temperatures generally between 100°C to 150°C
# - Critical parameter: minimize rate of rise to LESS THAN 2°C/second
PREHEAT_TEMP_MIN = 100  # °C

Processes thermocouple data, MES logs, and defect data to answer compliance questions
"""

import pandas as pd
import json
import os
import numpy as np
from collections import defaultdict

# Custom JSON encoder to handle numpy types
class NumpyEncoder(json.JSONEncoder):
    def default(self, obj):
        if isinstance(obj, (np.integer, np.int64)):
            return int(obj)
        if isinstance(obj, (np.floating, np.float64)):
            return float(obj)
        if isinstance(obj, np.ndarray):
            return obj.tolist()
        return super().default(obj)

# Create output directory
os.makedirs('/app/output', exist_ok=True)

# Load data

mes_log = pd.read_csv('/app/data/mes_log.csv')
thermocouples = pd.read_csv('/app/data/thermocouples.csv')
test_defects = pd.read_csv('/app/data/test_defects.csv')

print(f"Thermocouples: {len(thermocouples)} rows")
print(f"Test defects: {len(test_defects)} rows")

# QUESTION 1: Maximum Temperature Ramp Rate During Preheat
# ==============================================================================

print("QUESTION 1: Maximum Temperature Ramp Rate During Preheat")
print("="*80)

print(f"Ramp rate limit: {RAMP_RATE_LIMIT}°C/s")

    tc_ids = run_data['tc_id'].unique()

    max_ramp_per_tc = {}

    for tc_id in tc_ids:

            dtemp = preheat_data.iloc[i+1]['temp_c'] - preheat_data.iloc[i]['temp_c']
            if dt > 0:
                ramp_rate = dtemp / dt
                max_ramp = max(max_ramp, ramp_rate)

        max_ramp_per_tc[tc_id] = round(max_ramp, 2)

            "peak_temp_c": None,
            "required_min_peak_c": round(required_min_peak, 2)
        }

    tc1_data = run_data[run_data['tc_id'] == 'TC1']

    if len(tc1_data) == 0:
        # No TC1 data
        failing_runs.append(run_id)
        q3_results[run_id] = {
            "tc_id": None,

print(f"Output saved to /app/output/q03.json")

    actual_speed = row['conveyor_speed_cm_min']

    run_data = thermocouples[thermocouples['run_id'] == run_id]

    if len(run_data) > 0:
        # Total dwell time = max time in oven
        total_dwell_s = run_data['time_s'].max()

        # For proper reflow, we need:
        # - Time to reach preheat temp (100-150°C)
        # - Dryout/soak time
        # - Time above liquidus (30-60s)
        # - Cooling time
        # Typical total process time is 3-6 minutes based on industry standards

        # The required minimum speed ensures the board doesn't move too fast
        # Speed = Distance / Time
        # If board moves too fast, insufficient heating occurs

        # Based on the profile, minimum dwell should be ~180 seconds for proper reflow
        # This comes from: preheat (60s) + dryout (60s) + reflow (60s) minimum
        required_min_dwell_s = 180

        # But we should use actual achieved dwell if it worked
        # The actual speed already achieved this dwell, so it's the minimum
        # required_min_speed = (board_length / total_dwell_s) * 60  # cm/min

        # Actually, the constraint is that conveyor speed must be slow enough
        # to allow proper thermal dwell. So minimum speed is zero, and there's
        # a MAXIMUM speed constraint

        # Let me re-read the handbook requirement...
        # The requirement is about sizing the oven to avoid bottlenecks
        # But for thermal compliance, speed must be slow enough for proper heating

        # Without explicit constraints in handbook about max speed,
        # I'll use the requirement that total dwell must be >= 180s for complete profile
        required_min_speed = (board_length / required_min_dwell_s) * 60
    else:
        # No thermocouple data - cannot determine requirement
        required_min_speed = None

    meets = True
    if required_min_speed is not None and actual_speed is not None:
        # Speed must be >= minimum (fast enough to avoid jams)
        # but also slow enough for thermal dwell
        # Since we calculated min speed from required dwell,
        # actual speed should be <= max allowed for proper heating

        # Actually, let me reconsider: the question asks if speed is "feasible"
        # Feasible means it allows proper processing
        # Too fast = insufficient heating
        # Too slow = OK but inefficient

        # Calculate maximum allowable speed for minimum required dwell
        max_allowable_speed = (board_length / required_min_dwell_s) * 60

        if actual_speed > max_allowable_speed:

    q4_results.append({

    })

print("="*80)

with open('/app/output/q02.json', 'r') as f:
    q2_data = json.load(f)
with open('/app/output/q03.json', 'r') as f:
    q3_data = json.load(f)

q1_compliant = set([r for r in q1_data['max_ramp_by_run'].keys()
                    if r not in q1_data['violating_runs']])
q2_compliant = set([r['run_id'] for r in q2_data if r['status'] == 'compliant'])
q3_compliant = set([r for r in q3_data['min_peak_by_run'].keys()
                    if r not in q3_data['failing_runs']])

# Get yield data
yield_data = test_defects[test_defects['inspection_stage'] == 'SUMMARY']
yield_lookup = {}
for idx, row in yield_data.iterrows():
    yield_lookup[row['run_id']] = row['fp_yield_pct']

# Rank runs by board family
q5_results = []
board_families = mes_log['board_family'].unique()

for board_family in sorted(board_families):
    family_runs = mes_log[mes_log['board_family'] == board_family]['run_id'].tolist()

    # Score each run
    run_scores = []
    for run_id in family_runs:
        score = 0

        # Compliance checks (most important)
        compliant = (run_id in q1_compliant and
                    run_id in q2_compliant and
                    run_id in q3_compliant)

        if not compliant:
            # Non-compliant runs get negative score
            score -= 1000

        # Quality: yield percentage
        if run_id in yield_lookup:
            score += yield_lookup[run_id]

        # Efficiency: conveyor speed (higher is better for throughput)
        run_mes = mes_log[mes_log['run_id'] == run_id].iloc[0]
        speed = run_mes['conveyor_speed_cm_min']
        score += speed / 10  # Normalized contribution

        run_scores.append((run_id, score))

    # Sort by score (descending)
    run_scores.sort(key=lambda x: x[1], reverse=True)

    if len(run_scores) > 0:
        best_run = run_scores[0][0]
        runner_ups = [r[0] for r in run_scores[1:]]
    else:
        best_run = None
        runner_ups = []

    q5_results.append({
        "board_family": board_family,
        "best_run_id": best_run,
        "runner_up_run_ids": runner_ups
    })

# Sort by board_family
q5_results = sorted(q5_results, key=lambda x: x['board_family'])
